sources.title: Human History Map: Göktürk records and decoded map geometry
sources.note: Own-project factual-data exception. The established gokturk index spans 552-744 and imported maps show 600-800. The missing western-gokturk-khaganate record is only a 700-800 map snapshot. That late outline postdates the historical Western Turkic defeat in 657 and is treated publicly as a legacy/successor region.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Silk Roads Sites in Kyrgyzstan
sources.note: Official tentative-list dossier directly read. Chuy valley towns Navikat, Suyab and Balasagyn; mixed populations and cultures; Western Türk and Türgesh political importance c.560-760; Buddhist temples, a Zoroastrian fire altar/cemetery and Nestorian stones. Tentative status is not final World Heritage inscription.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Silk Roads, Chang’an-Tianshan Corridor
sources.note: Official inscription dossier directly read. Route network, forts, caravanserai, religious buildings, interdependence of nomadic and settled communities, and Zhetysu water-management systems. Broad corridor evidence is not attributed to every Turkic household.

sources.title: Étienne de la Vaissière, Sogdiana III: History and Archaeology, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis directly read. Turkic rule after c.560; Western khagans, On Oq and Türgesh in Semirechye; merchants, farmers and warriors in new settlements; elite intermarriage and cultural exchange. Tang claims and local political complexity are kept distinct.

sources.title: Étienne de la Vaissière, Sogdian Trade, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis directly read. Sogdian caravan merchants, Turkic protection and administration, 568-575 embassies to Byzantium, and loanwords linked with commercial practice. Sogdians are not described as the only traders or every Sogdian as a merchant.

sources.title: Larissa Baratova, Turko-Sogdian Coinage, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly numismatic article directly read. Sixth- to eighth-century issues, Sogdian and Bactrian legends, Turkic titles, tamgas and square-holed bronze forms. Coins support political/economic claims but are not modern territorial maps.

sources.title: S. Smailov and B. Kazmadiyarova, Coins of Turkic Khaganates from Taraz settlement (2025)
sources.note: Peer-reviewed original catalogue directly read. Exact published Sogdian transliteration on a Türgesh issue, find context and coin typology. The sample is a scholarly transliteration of a coin legend, not a Unicode facsimile of its letter shapes.

sources.title: UNESCO Silk Roads: Coin finds on the territory of Kyrgyzstan
sources.note: UNESCO-hosted scholarly chapter directly read. Türgesh legends, metrology, Sogdian writing and square-holed copper coins. Exact legend cross-checked with the 2025 Taraz catalogue.

sources.title: Étienne de la Vaissière, Central Asia X: Economy before the Timurids, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis directly read. Irrigation and trade expansion under western and eastern Turks; Chinese-source report of Sogdian boys learning books and commerce. This is an outsider’s generalized description, not proof of universal schooling.

sources.title: Gregory Semenov, Suyab, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly site history directly read. Sogdian foundation, Turkic and Chinese connections, religious remains, 738 Black Türgesh capital, 748 destruction and Karluk takeover in the 760s. A capital’s history does not represent every settlement.

sources.title: Kazuo Enoki and others, Khotan II: History in the Pre-Islamic Period, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly regional chronology directly read. Tang defeat of the Western Turks in 657 and subsequent contested protectorate claims. Tang suzerainty is not treated as continuous direct rule over the full atlas outline.

sources.title: C. E. Bosworth, Arab II: Arab conquest of Iran, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis directly read. Collapse of the western Turkish state in the mid-seventh century, political fragmentation and nominal Chinese backing among independent local states. Used to correct the atlas chronology, not to reduce the region to the history of conquest.

sources.title: Nicholas Sims-Williams, Chinese Turkestan VIII: Sogdian, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly language history directly read. Sogdian-derived writing, the Bugut inscription and Turkic titles including qaghan, tigin and tudun. Script relationships are described without claiming that all Turkic speakers wrote Sogdian.

sources.title: History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume III: The Türgesh state, UNESCO
sources.note: UNESCO scholarly volume, chapter pages 346 onward directly read. Türgesh formation from 699, Nevaket headquarters, twenty districts, Sogdian coin legend, Suluk’s reign and conflicts. Numerical troop capacities and propaganda language omitted.

sources.title: Peter B. Golden and C. Edmund Bosworth, Ghuzz, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis directly read. Eastern Türk chronology, Karluk migration into On Oq territory and takeover of Suyab in 766. The 766 date marks a political transfer, not disappearance of local people.

proposedOverrides.name: Western Turkic legacy and Türgesh successors
proposedOverrides.summary: The imported 700-800 outline postdates the historical Western Turkic defeat in 657 and is presented as an On Oq, Türgesh and Karluk successor landscape.

batchIdentityNotes: The historical Western Turkic khaganate was defeated in 657; the exact western-gokturk-khaganate polygon appears only in the 700 snapshot and is publicly qualified as a legacy/successor region.
The existing gokturk card was shallow and Wikipedia-only. This packet explicitly upgrades it and shares the revised card with the missing western snapshot record.
Eastern Second Turkic, western Türgesh and Karluk endings are separated; no single 744 or 800 collapse is imposed on all regions.
